newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Hashimoto urges greater Australian role in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Hashimoto urges greater Australian role in Asia.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Monday praised Australia's effort to forge closer ties with other Asian nations and urged that Canberra be admitted as a key member of a fledgling Asia-Europe forum.

"Australia should be praised for its determined and sincere efforts to build closer relations with Asian countries based on mutual understanding and trust, overcoming such differences in historical and cultural backgrounds," Hashimoto said in a speech at a parliamentary dinner in Canberra.
He added that Australia would make "outstanding contributions to the future development in the Asia-Pacific region".
"Japan, therefore, believes it is necessary for Australia to be welcomed to participate as an important member of the Asian side in the Asia-Europe Meeting," Hashimoto said.

Australia, embarrassed by its exclusion from the first Asia-Europe Meeting in Bangkok last year, has campaigned for entry into the forum, which links 10 Asian nations and the 15 members of the European Union.
Japan already had made clear that it suppported Canberra's membership, opposed primarily by Malaysia.
Australian Prime Minister John Howard said in return that Australia wanted to see a permanent Japanese seat on the U.N. Security Council.

"I would like to take this opportunity tonight, prime minister, to reaffirm the very strong support that my government extends to Japan's aspiration to become a permanent member of the Security Council of the United Nations," Howard said.

Hashimoto called for deeper ties between Japan and Australia, proposing annual summits between their leaders as a symbol of future cooperation on issues ranging from the economy and environment to security.

Hashimoto, fresh from a meeting with U.S. President Bill Clinton, reiterated Japan's stance that the U.S. military presence was vital to peace in the Asia-Pacific region and that the U.S.-Japan security arrangement was the pivotal framework for ensuring that presence.

While in Washington, Hashimoto assured Clinton that Japan was not seeking a cut in American military forces in Japan and Asia, despite calls for reductions of the U.S. presence by residents of Japan's island of Okinawa, where the bulk of U.S. military facilities is located.

Hashimoto welcomed Howard's visit to China earlier this year and both of them on Monday called for the development of deeper dialogue and cooperation with Beijing. Hashimoto is slated to visit Beijing later this year and to receive visits from Chinese leaders this year and next.

"I am of the view that the further promotion of bilateral relations among Japan, the United States, China and Australia will contribute greatly to the peace and prosperity of this region," Hashimoto said.

Hashimoto and many Japanese leaders are keen for Tokyo to raise its profile in Asia. But the nation remains divided over whether it should assume a higher-profile role in regional non-economic affairs, given constitutional limits on military action abroad and a traditional reliance on the U.S.-Japan security umbrella.
